newsitem.title: CHINA: China's Jiang travelling to Moscow to boost ties.
newsitem.headline: China's Jiang travelling to Moscow to boost ties.

text.p: Chinese President Jiang Zemin flies to Moscow this week to sign an historic troop reduction pact with Russia and Central Asian nations and to boost rapidly warming Sino-Russian ties. Jiang will meet Russian President Boris Yeltsin after he arrives in Moscow on April 22 for a five-day visit that diplomats said was aimed at keeping historically rocky relations on track following a successful summit in Beijing one year ago.

"It is... consolidating the progress they've made in the last couple years, giving the Chinese at least one major relationship in pretty good shape," said one diplomat, referring to China's difficulties with the United States, Europe and even some Asian neighbours.

Beijing and Moscow, staunch allies in the 1950s, saw relations plummet in following decades as the two wrangled over leadership of the communist world and fought skirmishes along the lengthy Sino-Soviet border.
Ties were largely restored when Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev visited China in 1989, and subsequent official exchanges have helped to put behind the era of distrust.

The centrepiece of Jiang's visit would be the signing of an accord to cut troop levels along the common borders of China, Russia, and central Asian states of Tajikistan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, a Russian embassy spokesman said.

"It will be a very important step towards building up some kind of scheme about an Asian security system," the spokesman said, adding that there were no plans for active military cooperation between China and Russia.

Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, who visited China last week, used his trip to defend Moscow's arms sales to China, saying weapons sold were defensive in nature and would not alter the balance of power in the Asia-Pacific region.
Rodionov's visit was the latest sign of warming ties between the two giants, but diplomats said decades of mistrust would prevent the creation of any new China-Russia axis.
"In spite of everything being so happy at the moment, it's nevertheless a tender relationship, and I think it's one that can slip off the rails quite easily," a diplomat said.

Beijing and Moscow would try to nurture what both sides have called a "strategic partnership" that was partly aimed at countering perceived threats from the United States and the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO), he said.
"The Chinese are trying to draw out the common ground here in terms of both sides, as the Chinese put it, dealing with U.S. hegemonism," the diplomat said.

Although China has insisted the newly forged relationship with Russia is not directed at any third country, Beijing definitely wanted to use Moscow to balance ties with Washington, which has clashed with China on issues from trade to human rights, he said.

"It (the partnership) is not explicitly directed against any country, but here are two countries that the Chinese at least see as having common ground in opposing what they think the Americans are doing," he said.
Moscow could also find in Beijing an ally against expansion plans into eastern Europe by NATO, he said.
"The Chinese aren't very happy about NATO expansion," he said. "It doesn't directly impinge on China's interests, but they're very uncomfortable with NATO expansion."
Jiang could also use the visit to fuel trade between the two powers, which Beijing says could reach $8-10 billion this year and hopes to boost to $20 billion by the end of the century.
"A lot of Sino-Russian trade is still sort of barter trade across the border and it has to be made into real trade to reach its potential," the diplomat said.
